paragraphs: Quickest changepoint detection concerns recognizing when a sequence changes its behavior. Two common evaluation measures are average run length and average detection delay. These are useful in theory and simulation, but real datasets introduce a complication: sequences may end before detection occurs, and different sequences may have different lengths. An evaluation must account for those unfinished observations.

The paper introduces KM-ARL and KM-ADD, non-parametric estimators built around an analogy with survival analysis. The relevant event is detection, and sequence truncation limits how long that event can be observed. This connection lets the estimators account for detection probabilities when the available observation windows are finite and irregular.

The authors derive bounds on estimation bias and prove asymptotic unbiasedness except when extrapolation is required. That qualification distinguishes estimating from observed follow-up from extending beyond it. Experiments on simulated and real datasets demonstrate more robust evaluation under limited sequence lengths, supporting clearer interpretation and practical detector selection.
icml-2026-accurate-evaluation-of-quickes.tldr: Survival-analysis estimators improve changepoint-detector evaluation when observation sequences are short or have unequal lengths.

paragraphs: Tree-search decoding gives a language model additional opportunities to explore reasoning paths before producing an answer. In deployment, however, each query may have a fixed allowance of generated tokens. A search policy that ignores the remaining allowance can spend its final tokens opening new branches or stop before developing a useful answer.

Budget-Guided MCTS makes the remaining token budget part of the search policy itself. It initially explores broadly, then shifts toward refining existing paths and completing answers as the available tokens decrease. It also reduces late branching from shallow nodes, where starting another path can consume resources that could otherwise finish ongoing reasoning.

The authors evaluate this approach with open-weight language models on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and an additional physics benchmark. They report consistent improvements over budget-agnostic tree-search baselines across inference budgets. The result supports adapting how search spends computation throughout a query, rather than relying only on a stopping rule when the token allowance runs out.
icml-2026-aligning-tree-search-policies-.tldr: BG-MCTS improves reasoning search by shifting from exploration toward answer completion as its token budget runs down.

paragraphs: Epidemic forecasts must cope with sparse observations and disease dynamics that change over time. Combining epidemiological models with learned patterns is appealing, but the paper argues that treating mechanistic estimates only as extra features or regularization can obscure their contribution. It can also leave the forecasting architecture predominantly dependent on patterns learned from data.

EpiDiff integrates mechanistic information into a diffusion forecasting process through uncertainty-aware steering at inference time. It estimates the posterior uncertainty of the mechanistic predictions and uses that uncertainty to vary their influence during generation. The contribution of epidemiological knowledge can therefore change with the confidence attached to its estimates.

Experiments on real-world datasets report consistently better accuracy and robustness than state-of-the-art baselines, particularly under changing distributions. EpiDiff also visualizes when forecasts rely on mechanistic laws versus data-driven patterns. This makes the combination more inspectable: the system exposes how its two sources of information contribute, alongside the reported predictive improvements.
icml-2026-bridging-dynamics-and-data-a-u.tldr: EpiDiff uses uncertainty in epidemiological estimates to steer diffusion forecasts, improving reported accuracy and robustness under changing disease dynamics.

paragraphs: Vision transformers need positional information that remains useful when images arrive at higher resolutions than those used during training. Rotary position embeddings encode location through rotations controlled by frequencies. Standard two-dimensional versions handle the image axes separately, while mixed versions combine them to represent diagonal relationships as well.

The authors observe that learned mixed frequencies can still favor particular directions because image features have an axial spectral bias. Compass-RoPE addresses this by describing frequencies through separate scales and angles. Uniformly initializing the angles across a full circle provides isotropic directional coverage at initialization. A further discrete Fourier transform mixing step enriches how multiple angles can be represented.

Experiments cover classification at multiple resolutions and dense prediction tasks. They show more stable extrapolation when image resolution changes substantially. The contribution is a more deliberate treatment of direction in positional encoding: representing diagonals alone does not resolve the observed imbalance, so Compass-RoPE explicitly organizes frequency directions and expands their angular expressiveness.
icml-2026-compass-rope-isotropic-rotary-.tldr: Compass-RoPE reorganizes positional frequencies by scale and angle to improve vision-transformer stability across large resolution changes.

paragraphs: Different language models can fail on different parts of the same reasoning problem. CoRe turns this complementarity into a training signal. Models first attempt a problem independently. In a second round, unsuccessful models receive a hint extracted from a successful peer and get an opportunity to recover.

Training combines rewards for correctness, diversity, and successful rescue. The diversity term encourages models to avoid overlapping errors, while the rescue bonus rewards useful learning from peer hints. Together, these objectives encourage both independent strengths and productive collaboration, rather than evaluating only whether each isolated attempt succeeds.

With 1,000 training examples, a 3B-plus-4B model pair achieves oracle Team Pass@2 of 99.54% on GSM8K and 92.08% on MATH. These are team results with oracle selection, not individual-model accuracy. The paper also reports results on GPQA and AIME. In a three-model AIME evaluation, majority voting reaches 81.20%, compared with 82.60% oracle Team Pass@2, showing that much of the team benefit persists without oracle selection in that setting.
icml-2026-core-collaborative-reasoning-v.tldr: CoRe trains models to learn from successful peers while preserving complementary strengths, producing large reported gains in team reasoning.

paragraphs: Upcycling expands a pretrained dense model into a sparse mixture of experts, increasing capacity while reusing existing weights. A problem arises when experts begin as simple copies: they may fail to develop distinct specialties. The router, which assigns inputs to experts, is therefore an important place to influence how specialization develops.

Dirichlet-Prior Shaping Loss regularizes the router's probability distributions by matching expert assignments to a target Dirichlet prior. That target can express preferences for how experts should divide work, including specialization by modality or task. The intended division is encoded in the training objective, allowing specialization to emerge without manually intervening in individual assignments.

Experiments on upcycled vision-language models report consistent improvements over the compared upcycling strategies and regularization methods across standard benchmarks. The paper also presents the loss as applicable beyond expert routing, to modules that output categorical probabilities. Its central contribution is a way to guide the shape of assignment distributions directly and thereby encourage more useful differentiation among initially similar experts.
icml-2026-dirichlet-prior-shaping-guidin.tldr: DPSL shapes routing probabilities with a Dirichlet prior to encourage specialization and improve upcycled vision-language mixture-of-experts models.

paragraphs: Translating a written optimization problem into executable mathematics requires more than producing valid code. A program can run successfully while representing the wrong constraints or objective, yielding an invalid result without a syntax error. This paper addresses those silent formulation failures through a learned drafting and auditing workflow.

Draft-and-Audit RL uses a shared-parameter policy for two stages: constructing a draft and revising it through an audit. Training rewards depend solely on execution of the final audited program. Intermediate solver feedback does not guide the repairs, so the policy must learn to perform rubric-guided revision within the workflow itself.

This final-only reward links the quality of drafting to the success of later correction. The paper argues that the setup encourages cross-turn synergy: drafts can become structured in ways that make their errors easier for the same policy to repair. The proposed contribution is thus a training formulation for optimization modeling that treats self-revision and the preparation of revisable drafts as connected capabilities.
icml-2026-draft-and-audit-reinforcement-.tldr: Draft-and-Audit RL trains a shared policy to write and revise optimization programs using rewards from only the final audited execution.

paragraphs: Open-ended learning requires agents to keep acquiring abilities across an expanding range of challenges. Generating many environments does not by itself provide a useful learning progression. In complex worlds, the space of possible challenges is so large that an agent can struggle to encounter intermediate experiences that connect its current abilities to harder skills.

Dreaming in Code uses foundation models to generate executable variations of an environment. These code-level changes serve as a curriculum: they create intermediate worlds intended to scaffold increasing competence. The framework makes environment construction part of controlling the learning sequence, with emphasis on sustained progression rather than the discovery of isolated behaviors.

The authors instantiate the approach in Craftax, an open-ended benchmark with rich mechanics and long-horizon progression. They report a 17% improvement in mean return over the strongest baseline and non-zero success on late-game combat tasks where prior methods fail. These findings suggest that executable environment variations can bridge competence gaps and help agents acquire skills requiring longer sequences of progress.
icml-2026-dreaming-in-code-for-curriculu.tldr: Dreaming in Code generates executable environment variations that scaffold learning and improve long-horizon skill acquisition in Craftax.

paragraphs: Analogical reasoning transfers a relational pattern from one domain to another. This paper gives that ability a concrete formulation for transformers: inferring correspondences between entities in different categories. The formulation draws inspiration from functors in category theory, providing a basis for synthetic tasks where the emergence of analogy can be studied under controlled conditions.

The experiments find that analogical reasoning is sensitive to the characteristics of the training data, optimization choices, and model scale. Mechanistic analysis separates the observed ability into two components. First, relational structures become geometrically aligned in the embedding space. Second, the transformer applies a functor that transfers structure between the categories.

This account connects successful analogy to both representation geometry and an operation performed within the network. The authors quantify the effects and observe the same trends in pretrained language models. The findings provide a mechanistic explanation for the studied behavior while emphasizing that its emergence depends strongly on the learning setup, rather than following automatically from using a transformer.
icml-2026-emergent-analogical-reasoning-.tldr: Controlled tasks and mechanistic analysis connect transformer analogy to aligned relational geometry and structure transfer across categories.

paragraphs: Choosing the mixture of pretraining data depends on having categories that reflect useful semantic differences. Human taxonomies can misalign with the data, while ordinary Euclidean clustering can struggle when embeddings are distributed unevenly across directions. GEM addresses the representation of data categories as a foundation for deciding how much training material to draw from each.

The framework formulates curation as a variational problem on a hypersphere and adds a regularizer that encourages balanced mixing. It separates the generative prior and uses a Minorize-Maximize optimization algorithm with theoretical support. This design counters cluster collapse and discovers balanced semantic structure. Teacher-student distillation scales the approach to web-sized corpora, while a Geometric Influence Score supports interpretable taxonomy construction.

Experiments with 1.1B-parameter language models integrate GEM into DoReMi and RegMix mixing strategies. The authors report state-of-the-art results in that evaluation, including improvements of up to 1.2% in average downstream accuracy. The findings connect better geometric organization of the corpus with more effective and interpretable choices about pretraining composition.
icml-2026-gem-geometric-entropy-mixing-f.tldr: GEM learns balanced semantic categories on a hypersphere to improve data mixing and reported downstream performance in language-model pretraining.

paragraphs: Targeted instruction tuning seeks a small set of training examples that will help a particular task. Many selection methods estimate an example's influence using optimizer statistics that scale parameter coordinates independently. The paper shows that this approximation breaks down in parameter-efficient tuning such as LoRA, where updates have substantial interactions across parameters.

GIST uses the observation that task-relevant update directions occupy a low-dimensional subspace. It applies singular value decomposition to validation gradients to identify that subspace, then projects candidate training gradients into it. Examples receive scores according to their alignment with target directions. This captures coupled update directions instead of representing the geometry only through separate coordinate scales.

Under the same selection budget, the reported experiments match or outperform the state-of-the-art baseline while using 0.29% of its storage and 25% of its computational time. The result suggests that accounting for parameter interactions need not require retaining a large, detailed representation of all updates: a task-specific subspace can provide an effective and much smaller basis for selection.
icml-2026-gist-targeted-data-selection-f.tldr: GIST selects instruction-tuning data through task-specific gradient subspaces, matching or improving reported performance with far less storage and computation.

paragraphs: Human ranking feedback often reveals only part of an ordering, leaving the learner to identify the best items from incomplete comparisons. Existing methods commonly make restrictive assumptions about both the distribution generating rankings and the process hiding parts of them. The paper develops a broader framework for learning the top-k items under incomplete feedback.

Its ranking models must satisfy a property called complete consensus, a class that includes the widely used Plackett-Luce and Mallows models. Its positional censoring model broadens the ways preferences determine what becomes visible, encompassing winner-only and top-h feedback. These two choices allow the framework to unify and strictly generalize established settings.

The authors introduce PIRATE and prove a near-optimal, instance-dependent sample-complexity bound. This characterizes how much feedback is needed in relation to the particular ranking problem. Under Plackett-Luce rankings, PIRATE also matches state-of-the-art sample complexity in the relevant winner and top-h settings. The broader assumptions therefore retain strong guarantees in familiar special cases.
icml-2026-learning-to-rank-from-incomple.tldr: PIRATE learns top-ranked items under a broader model of incomplete feedback while retaining near-optimal sample-complexity guarantees.

paragraphs: Questions involving exclusions are difficult for systems that translate language into knowledge-graph queries. A negative condition may apply to just one branch of a question or to particular supporting paths. If that scope is lost during translation or execution, the system can exclude the wrong answers or retain answers that should have been ruled out.

The paper introduces an Executable Exchange Contract between a component that specifies the query and one that executes it. The contract makes exclusion scope explicit as executable control information. MatLogic, the executor, converts those exclusions into local masks used during multi-hop propagation. Its execution schedule applies exclusions before supporting evidence is lost or separate branches become entangled.

The system can additionally return compact pointers to witnesses, preserving distinctions among support types when needed. Evaluation covers structured complex queries and complete natural-language question answering. Contract-aligned diagnostics separate specification mistakes from execution mistakes and test the necessity of scoped enforcement, making the interface useful for both carrying out exclusions and locating where a query goes wrong.
icml-2026-llm-matlogic-executable-exchan.tldr: LLM-MatLogic makes exclusion scope executable so knowledge-graph queries enforce negative conditions on the intended branches and evidence paths.

paragraphs: Long-context pretraining is expensive because standard attention costs grow quadratically with sequence length. This becomes a bottleneck when training on material such as entire code repositories or collections of related documents. Multipole Semantic Attention, or MuSe, approximates attention during training to reduce that cost while retaining useful access to long contexts.

MuSe groups queries and keys separately in representation space and constructs summaries tailored to the queries. The grouping is therefore based on learned representations rather than only where tokens sit in the sequence. At matched sparsity, the authors report that these summaries substantially outperform spatial blocking. The method requires no architectural changes.

Pretraining experiments on code and scientific documents use models up to 1B parameters with 64k contexts. MuSe accelerates this training by 36% while matching baseline loss and preserving reported quality and long-context utilization. The authors also validate compatibility with existing Llama 3.1-8B and 3.2-1B models without retraining, supporting its use as a drop-in attention approximation.
icml-2026-multipole-semantic-attention-a.tldr: MuSe uses semantic query and key clustering to accelerate reported 64k-context pretraining by 36% while matching baseline loss.

paragraphs: Large multimodal models combine encoders for individual modalities with language models, but understanding their internal representations through explicit logic remains difficult. This paper proposes learning token representations through a neuro-fuzzy framework so that the resulting concepts can be interpreted in terms of rules, rather than only inspected as hidden numerical features.

The method uses fuzzy rules to calculate activation firing strengths, expressing the degree to which rules activate. A defuzzification step then extracts distinct concepts from those activations. This process connects learned representations to explicit logic and produces multimodal concepts that the authors describe as semantically coherent and interpretable.

Qualitative and quantitative experiments demonstrate the concepts' usefulness for interpreting test samples. The evaluation also examines disentanglement, or how separately the concepts represent different factors, and their grounding in both visual and textual information. These checks address whether the extracted concepts provide meaningful handles on multimodal representations across the two domains. The contribution is a representation-learning mechanism that incorporates interpretable rules into concept formation.
icml-2026-neuro-fuzzy-concept-learning-f.tldr: A neuro-fuzzy framework turns rule activations into interpretable multimodal concepts and evaluates their usefulness, disentanglement, and visual-textual grounding.

paragraphs: Generating a solution to a partial differential equation requires consistency with both the governing equation and any available observations. The paper introduces a diffusion sampling method that incorporates these requirements into generation. Its aim is to produce solution fields that remain physically admissible while using a generative model to construct them.

The guidance comes from PDE residuals and observational constraints. Residuals express discrepancies with the governing equations, while observational constraints connect a candidate field to measured information. The method uses these signals to guide stochastic sampling and embeds that sampling procedure in a new Sequential Monte Carlo framework, yielding a scalable generative PDE solver.

Evaluation spans multiple benchmark PDE systems, including multiphysics settings and systems of interacting PDEs. Across those evaluations, the authors report lower numerical error than existing state-of-the-art generative methods. The findings support combining diffusion generation with explicit physical and observational guidance. They concern the quality of generated solution fields across the tested systems, including settings involving multiple interacting physical equations.
icml-2026-particle-guided-diffusion-mode.tldr: Physics-guided diffusion sampling within a Sequential Monte Carlo framework produces PDE solution fields with lower reported numerical error.

paragraphs: Hierarchies must represent both what concepts mean and how they relate directionally, such as which concept is a parent of another. Polaris separates these roles using angular geometry for semantics and radius for hierarchical structure. This addresses the difficulty of learning asymmetric relationships when semantic information is noisy.

The framework constructs spherical representations by projecting into a tangent space at the north pole and applying an exponential map. Spherical linear layers maintain unit-norm representations. Training combines local constraints, global regularization against geometric collapse, and uncertainty-aware asymmetric objectives that encourage directional containment. At inference, structure-guided retrieval narrows the candidate parents before the final ranking step.

The authors evaluate taxonomy expansion for trees, hierarchies with multiple parents, and multimodal hierarchies. Across these settings, they report consistent improvements over fourteen strong baselines, reaching approximately 19 points in top-K retrieval and approximately 60% reduction in mean rank. The results support explicitly separating semantic geometry from hierarchical position while using the hierarchy itself to guide retrieval.
icml-2026-polaris-coupled-orbital-polar-.tldr: Polaris separates meaning and hierarchy in polar embeddings, improving reported parent retrieval across several taxonomy-expansion settings.

paragraphs: Streaming video systems may receive a question long after the relevant visual event has passed. With bounded GPU memory, a briefly visible clue can disappear as newer tokens arrive. ProtoKV addresses this delayed-query problem by maintaining a fixed-size representation of distant history alongside an exact cache for the recent video window.

Older information is aggregated into a bank of semantic-spatial prototypes with residual statistics. This bank summarizes history rather than preserving selected old token instances. When a query arrives, each prototype is presented through a bounded pseudo-token interface compatible with standard attention. The design keeps historical memory capacity fixed while allowing the model to attend to its summarized contents.

On streaming-video benchmarks, ProtoKV improves accuracy by up to 12.5 points over token-retention baselines in the long-delay regime. These comparisons use matched budgets and comparable query-time cost, and the gains increase with query delay. The results suggest that summary-state memory can retain useful historical evidence more effectively than the compared retention methods as the gap between observation and question grows.
icml-2026-protokv-streaming-video-unders.tldr: ProtoKV summarizes older video in fixed-capacity prototypes to improve delayed-query answering under matched memory and query-time budgets.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction methods are commonly assessed by whether their intervals achieve the intended coverage and how short those intervals are. This paper shows why that pair of measurements can be misleading. A method can preserve marginal coverage and potentially reduce measured interval length while giving inconsistent outputs for exactly the same input.

The authors construct a procedure called the Prejudicial Trick. For each test sample, it randomly returns either a null interval or an interval built with an adjusted confidence level. This preserves marginal coverage, but repeated runs can yield completely different intervals. The authors formally derive conditions under which the procedure produces deceptively favorable interval-length results.

Experiments across regression and classification tasks provide empirical evidence for this behavior. The paper introduces interval stability as an additional metric to help detect improvements arising from similar techniques. The implication is that valid aggregate coverage and shorter intervals can coexist with undesirable run-to-run variability, so the meaning of an apparent efficiency gain depends on more than those two standard measures.
icml-2026-questioning-the-coverage-lengt.tldr: A randomized construction shows that conformal intervals can appear shorter while retaining coverage yet becoming unstable across repeated runs.

paragraphs: Optimal transport provides a principled way to map between distributions, with applications in generative modeling. Neural approaches learn reusable maps that can be evaluated on new samples, but existing methods are tailored to Euclidean geometry. This paper considers transport on Riemannian manifolds, where the geometry of the space must be respected.

The authors first prove a dimensionality barrier: methods producing discrete approximations of manifold transport maps require exponentially many parameters in the manifold dimension to achieve fixed accuracy. They introduce Riemannian Neural Optimal Transport maps as continuous neural parameterizations that avoid discretization and incorporate the geometry by construction.

Under mild regularity assumptions, the proposed maps approximate Riemannian optimal transport maps with sub-exponential complexity in dimension. The assumptions qualify the favorable approximation guarantee; it is not an unrestricted claim about every transport problem. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate improved scalability and competitive performance against discretization-based baselines, connecting the theoretical motivation to observed computational behavior.
icml-2026-riemannian-neural-optimal-tran.tldr: Continuous geometry-aware neural transport maps achieve sub-exponential approximation complexity under regularity assumptions and improve reported scalability on manifolds.

paragraphs: Small, sparse structures are difficult to segment in large images because full-resolution processing is expensive and most voxels belong to other classes. Downsampling or fixed region construction can weaken the boundary evidence needed for those minority structures. SEMIR learns a compact graph representation adapted to the segmentation target.

Starting from the image's grid graph, SEMIR contracts edges and deletes nodes and edges to construct a boundary-aligned graph minor. It preserves an exact map for lifting graph predictions back to grid labels. A few-shot structure-learning objective uses boundary Dice to align the representation with target-specific semantic edges. Geometric and intensity descriptors then support region-level inference with a graph neural network.

Experiments on BraTS 2021, KiTS23, and LiTS report consistent improvements in minority-structure Dice at practical runtime. The representation moves inference away from the native grid while retaining an exact decoding route; exact decoding here concerns mapping predictions back to labels, rather than guaranteeing correct segmentation. The findings support learning the computational representation around boundaries that matter for the target.
icml-2026-semir-semantic-minor-induced-r.tldr: SEMIR learns compact boundary-aligned graphs with exact label lifting, improving reported segmentation of minority structures at practical runtime.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction is often evaluated by averaging over possible calibration datasets. In practice, a user may have only one small calibration set, and the resulting prediction-set sizes can depend strongly on which observations it contains. The paper identifies this variability as a particular concern for methods that localize their predictions.

The authors formalize set stability as the variance, across calibration data, of the conditional expected set size. This separates stability with respect to the available calibration sample from performance averaged over many such samples. They propose Stable Conformal Prediction, a transfer-learning approach using labeled source-task data and unlabeled target data to improve stability without acquiring additional target-task labels.

Theoretical analysis characterizes the method's marginal coverage and stability. Empirically, it produces more stable prediction sets than standard conformal methods when calibration data are limited, especially for localized methods. The contribution addresses how reliably a method behaves with the particular calibration set a practitioner actually has, alongside the usual aggregate assessment of prediction quality.
icml-2026-stable-localized-conformal-pre.tldr: StCP uses source-task labels and unlabeled target data to reduce prediction-set variability caused by small calibration samples.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks have discrete firing events that make ordinary differentiation difficult. Training commonly substitutes heuristic surrogate gradients for those events. UltraLIF instead derives differentiable neuron dynamics through ultradiscretization, connecting continuous relaxations with discrete threshold behavior using the max-plus algebra of tropical geometry.

Its soft maximum is a log-sum-exp function controlled by a learnable temperature. As that temperature approaches zero, the function approaches hard thresholding. The paper derives UltraLIF from temporal leaky-integrate-and-fire dynamics and UltraDLIF from a diffusion equation describing spatial coupling among neurons. Both support standard backpropagation without using different forward and backward models. The analysis establishes pointwise convergence, quantitative error bounds, and bounded non-vanishing gradients.

Across six benchmarks covering static images, neuromorphic vision, and audio, the authors report improvements over surrogate-gradient baselines. Gains are strongest in the single-step, ultra-low-latency setting on neuromorphic and temporal datasets. An optional sparsity penalty also reduces energy use while preserving competitive accuracy, linking the differentiable formulation to both predictive and efficiency benefits in the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-ultralif-fully-differentiable-.tldr: UltraLIF derives differentiable spiking dynamics that approach hard thresholds, improving reported accuracy and enabling energy reductions through optional sparsity.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning produces useful representations without relying on conventional task labels, but its many methods lack a single explanatory framework. This paper casts them as latent distribution matching. Representations are trained to have high probability under an assumed latent model while also maintaining high entropy, which prevents collapse to uninformative representations.

These two aims correspond to alignment and uniformity. The framework connects independent component analysis with contrastive, non-contrastive, and predictive methods, including approaches using stop gradients. By expressing them through a common objective, it makes their underlying assumptions more explicit and provides a basis for designing methods from a specified latent model.

The authors use the framework to derive a nonlinear Bayesian filtering model for high-dimensional time series, with a Kalman-based predictor and no sampling requirement. They also prove that predictive latent distribution matching yields identifiable representations under mild assumptions, even with nonlinear predictors. The contribution therefore combines a unifying interpretation with a concrete model derivation and a conditional theoretical guarantee about recovering latent representations.
icml-2026-understanding-self-supervised-.tldr: Latent distribution matching unifies self-supervised objectives and yields a sampling-free filtering model plus conditional identifiability guarantees.

paragraphs: Spending additional computation at inference time can improve language-model reasoning, but search strategies must fit the model's generation process. Masked diffusion language models generate through iterative unmasking rather than a strictly left-to-right sequence. UnMaskFork uses that structure to search over alternative paths through generation.

The framework treats an unmasking trajectory as a tree and applies Monte Carlo Tree Search to optimize the path. Its branches come from deterministic partial-unmasking actions performed by multiple masked diffusion models. This makes the choice of how to reveal a partial answer an explicit search decision, providing an alternative to expanding candidates through stochastic sampling alone.

Empirical evaluation reports consistent improvements over existing test-time scaling baselines on complex coding benchmarks and strong scalability on mathematical reasoning tasks. These findings support using the iterative, non-autoregressive structure of masked diffusion as a basis for more advanced search. The contribution concerns organizing additional inference computation around generation trajectories, with the reported benefits demonstrated on coding and mathematical reasoning.
icml-2026-unmaskfork-test-time-scaling-f.tldr: UnMaskFork searches deterministic partial-unmasking trajectories to improve masked-diffusion reasoning with additional inference computation.
